criterion_notes.c1: The paper conceptually discusses household and community access to sanitation and drinking water services within the framing of the human right to sanitation (HRS) and human right to water and sanitation (HRWS).
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper clearly discusses legal, institutional, regulatory, and governance frameworks (international treaties, UN resolutions, national recognition, accountability mechanisms, and non-state actor regulation). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, it also touches conceptually on rule-type mechanisms governing access—such as tariff structures/cost recovery, tenure insecurity in informal settlements, and legal enforcement mechanisms—though mainly within a broad doctrinal and normative literature overview rather than an empirical evaluation of a specific rule. Regardless of whether Criterion 2 is read broadly or narrowly, the paper fails Criterion 3 (no empirical evidence).
criterion_notes.c3: Excluded under E05: this is a narrative multidisciplinary WIREs Water Overview of legal and non-legal scholarship (1990-2015) compiled broadly from Google Scholar, Wiley Online, and Science Direct. It presents no primary empirical data and is not a systematic empirical synthesis (no search strategy, eligibility criteria, study selection count, quality appraisal, or structured synthesis of empirical findings).
criterion_notes.c4: Does not measure or synthesize empirical access outcomes; it summarizes normative human rights standards (availability, safety, acceptability, accessibility, affordability) and conceptual indicator frameworks from secondary literature.
criterion_notes.c5: As a non-systematic conceptual and doctrinal literature overview without empirical data, no empirical study population, unit of analysis, exposure, or empirical outcome design is identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Obani and Gupta (2016) is a conceptual and doctrinal WIREs Water Overview comparing themes in the legal and non-legal literature on the human right to sanitation (HRS) and human right to water and sanitation (HRWS). Although it discusses sanitation access and legal/regulatory concepts (including cost recovery, tariffs, tenure security, and accountability mechanisms), it contains no primary empirical data and is a narrative overview rather than a systematic empirical synthesis. It is therefore excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
